speaker: Guillermo Rauch
title: A conversation with Vercel's Guillermo Rauch
question: In B2B and AI software, how does the rise of conversational AI interfaces change the protocols products need to reach users?
guest: If the programming language of tomorrow is human, that means you will likely be integrated into the places where conversations are already happening. If you and I are chatting on WhatsApp, we might create a group with a bot in WhatsApp, or in Slack, the same thing. The interface that has been the poster child of this first era of AI is conversation—talking to agents and prompting—and I expect that to continue. What is also true is that a lot of these platforms already exist: ChatGPT, Grok, v0, Cursor. So you have to pay attention to the protocols that allow you to meet customers where they are. Literally this morning I got a pitch from a data AI company where the founder made the case that one of the key interfaces for his product is going to be the MCP server. A lot of enterprises are building their own internal ChatGPTs—we have one at Vercel, Stripe has one, Shopify has one—so your product might not have a pixel interface per se. You might just tell a company, "If you connect to our MCP server, you are going to get this value from us."

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
As conversational AI becomes the place where people get work done, products increasingly have to reach users through an assistant or agent, not just through their own graphical interface. That shifts the critical integration layer from human-facing UIs and bespoke REST integrations toward machine-readable, agent-facing protocols.

The most prominent is the Model Context Protocol (MCP), introduced by Anthropic in 2024 and since adopted by OpenAI, Google, Microsoft and others. It standardizes how a product exposes tools, data and prompts to any compliant AI client. Alongside it sit agent-to-agent protocols such as Google's A2A for cross-vendor agent coordination, and emerging commerce and payment protocols for agent-initiated transactions.

For B2B vendors, the practical consequences are several. A well-documented API is no longer enough; products need an MCP server or equivalent with clear tool descriptions that models can reason about. Authentication has to support delegated, scoped access, typically OAuth, so that agents act on a user's behalf. And distribution increasingly runs through assistant app directories and connectors, making discoverability by models a new channel alongside SEO and marketplaces.

The risk for those who don't adapt is disintermediation, where the assistant owns the user relationship.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
Historically, B2B software reached users directly through browser interfaces over HTTP and integrated with other systems via deterministic REST or GraphQL APIs wired ahead of time by developers. As conversational AI assistants become the primary enterprise workspace, vendors can no longer assume users will visit standalone applications; instead, products must become dynamically discoverable, callable, and renderable inside the chat hosts and agents where users already work.

That shift replaces static endpoints with semantic, stateful protocols. Products now expose self-describing tools and live context through the Model Context Protocol (MCP) so models can discover and invoke capabilities at runtime, while Agent2Agent (A2A) lets a user’s primary assistant delegate complex work to a vendor’s specialized agent. When enterprise workflows outgrow plain text, generative interface protocols like MCP Apps, A2UI, and AG-UI stream interactive views directly into the conversation. Underneath, scoped OAuth 2.1 delegation and agentic payment standards let intermediaries enforce enterprise permissions and transact safely on a user’s behalf.

Instead, software must adopt agent-native protocols—such as the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and agent-to-agent standards—that make capabilities directly discoverable and executable by language models. Unlike conventional APIs built for deterministic code, these protocols pair structured schemas with rich semantic descriptions, teaching AI intermediaries when and how to invoke tools, pull context, and orchestrate workflows on a user's behalf. Because users increasingly stay inside unified AI assistants rather than switching SaaS tabs, protocols must also support stateful, bidirectional communication for streaming progress, human-in-the-loop confirmations, and inline UI components rendered directly in chat. Simultaneously, authentication protocols must evolve from static API keys or browser sessions to scoped, delegated authorization that enforces each employee's exact permissions across autonomous actions. Ultimately, reaching users shifts from capturing human clicks to speaking standardized, self-describing protocols that turn any AI host into a distribution channel for your product.

That means B2B vendors increasingly need to ship an MCP server alongside their REST API. For agents working across company boundaries, Google's Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol handles discovery and delegation. In commerce, protocols such as OpenAI and Stripe's Agentic Commerce Protocol and Google's AP2 let agents complete purchases.

The practical effect is that distribution moves away from SEO, app stores and polished screens toward being chosen by a model. That rewards clear tool descriptions, structured outputs, scoped permissions and actions that are safe to retry. It also brings new requirements: OAuth for agents acting on a user's behalf, audit trails, and pricing for usage driven by agents. Products that can't be called by an AI client risk becoming hidden back ends behind someone else's assistant.

noweb.answer:
Historically, B2B software reached users through web GUIs for humans and rigid REST or GraphQL APIs for pre-coded integrations. As conversational AI interfaces and autonomous agents become the primary layer through which users work, products can no longer rely on users visiting standalone apps. Instead, they must adopt protocols designed for dynamic, machine-mediated discovery and execution.

First, products need standardized tool and context protocols—such as the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and semantically rich OpenAPI schemas—so AI assistants can discover capabilities, understand parameters, and invoke actions reliably at runtime without custom glue code. Second, because agents act on users' behalf across multiple systems, products require finer-grained delegated authentication, permission scoping, and audit protocols (extending OAuth and agent-to-agent standards) to enforce enterprise security. Finally, streaming and structured UI protocols allow products to render interactive cards, approvals, and live updates directly inside the conversation rather than forcing context switches. Ultimately, reaching users shifts from optimizing human navigation to exposing secure, self-describing, agent-ready interfaces.

When users ask an AI assistant to do work, the assistant becomes another way to reach them. A buyer might say “update the renewal forecast” without opening the CRM or naming a product. To serve that request, the software needs a way for the assistant to discover what it can do, understand what inputs it needs, and act with the buyer’s permissions.
